title: Has Microsoft Stock Run Ahead Of Its AI Payoff?
detail:
Has Microsoft Stock Run Ahead Of Its AI Payoff?
Trefis Team
Fri, August 28, 2026 at 4:10 PM MDT 4 min read

AAPL
ORCL
Explore stocks on Coinbase

Image by Pexels from Pixabay

The software giant's stock has a powerful business engine behind its long-term trend, but a rapid run-up back toward all-time highs forces investors to ask if the price of admission is still worth paying.

Microsoft (MSFT) has built one of the most durable cash-generation engines in enterprise technology, but its stock currently trades about 6% below its 52-week high. For any investor sizing up the company's dominant push into artificial intelligence, the central question is clear: is this a consolidation pause before another leg higher, or has the current price already captured the payoff? While the stock's broader trend strength ranks near the middle of US-listed stocks above $1B, the recent rally to within 6% of its 52-week high brings the core tension into focus: does the fundamental engine justify the elevated valuation?

The core investment case rests on this underlying operational momentum rather than technical strength, raising the question of whether the current price offers sufficient upside for new buyers.

Is This a Genuine Business Surge?

The numbers behind Microsoft's run are strong. The company's operating margin over the last twelve months is a huge 47%, far outpacing the S&P 500 median of 18.5%. This isn't a one-time event; its three-year average is similarly high. Revenue growth tells the same story, at 17.8% over the past year, more than double the 8.3% median for the index.

This financial power comes directly from its strategic execution in AI and cloud computing. In its most recent quarter, revenue from Azure and other cloud services grew 43%, a clear sign that demand for its AI services is intense. Management confirmed that "Customer demand continues to exceed available capacity." The adoption of its AI tools is also rapid, with the company reporting it now has "over 30 million paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats."

What Does a Share of This Engine Cost?

The market is well aware of this operational strength, and it charges a premium. Microsoft trades at a price-to-earnings multiple of 28.0, compared to an S&P 500 median of 23.3. That premium exists even after a stretch of relative underperformance: over the trailing twelve months, Microsoft has been largely flat, trailing the S&P 500's +21% return. The stock also trades about 6% below its two-year high of $537.65, reinforcing that buyers today are not chasing a fresh peak.

The primary risk centers on the sheer scale of capital expenditure required to sustain this AI buildout. Some analysts are asking if soaring capital expenditures could put the stock's valuation at risk. The concern is that the company is building for a level of demand that might not materialize, or that rising component costs could squeeze profitability. This risk is compounded by declines in legacy businesses. Management expects revenue from its Windows OEM and Devices segment to "decline in the high teens for the fiscal year," and Xbox revenue recently decreased 10%. For investors who prefer broader exposure to the technology sector without concentrating on a single company's execution risk, a technology ETF like VGT might be an alternative.

The video-call giant is generating far more cash than the average company, yet the market is treating it like a business in decline. Here's the offer on the table.

The market is offering a cash machine at a discount, which raises the central question for any investor: is this a high-yield bargain, or is the market correctly pricing in a future breakdown?

The cash flow is built on a profitable, expanding platform. Zoom (ZM)'s ability to generate cash is not a recent fluke. The company has produced positive free cash flow in every twelve-month period for the last three years, totaling $1.93 billion in the most recent stretch. This is the output of a highly profitable operation, with a trailing operating margin of 24%, well above the 18.5% S&P 500 median. The balance sheet is also clean, with net cash of about $7.2 billion, meaning the high yield isn't an illusion created by debt. The machine behind these numbers is Zoom's strategic shift from a single-product application to an integrated communications platform.

While revenue growth of 5.0% over the last year trails the 8.3% median for large companies, management is focused on selling a broader "AI-first system of action." This includes products like Zoom Phone and Zoom Contact Center, which are driving larger, multi-year deals with corporate clients. The market is pricing a gap between new wins and existing customer spend. The offer exists because the market sees a contradiction in Zoom's story. On one hand, the push into the enterprise is showing clear results. Enterprise revenue recently grew 7.8%, its strongest rate in three years. The company's remaining performance obligations, which represent future contracted revenue, jumped 14% to $4.5 billion, signaling success in landing bigger commitments.

But there is a catch. The company's trailing 12-month net dollar expansion rate for enterprise customers was 99%. In simple terms, for every dollar Zoom received from its existing enterprise clients a year ago, it now gets 99 cents. Upsells and cross-sells are being slightly offset by churn and downgrades. This creates a difficult situation where growth depends heavily on winning new customers, because the current base isn't expanding its spend. Compounding this, management's latest outlook assumes "flat online growth," putting the full weight of the company's future on that enterprise segment. The entire offer hinges on turning new platform deals into net expansion. The debate over Zoom's value boils down to this tension. The company is a cash-rich, highly profitable business that is successfully winning larger deals with new enterprise customers. Yet it has not yet proven it can consistently expand spending within its existing customer base.

But for a company whose stock has run so far, its price tag seems disconnected from its performance. BlackBerry carries the richest valuation in its peer group while ranking last on growth and margins. Has the market correctly anticipated a turnaround before it shows up in reported earnings, or is it getting ahead of fundamentals?

Why does BlackBerry carry a richer valuation than software and tech peers

By comparative metrics, BlackBerry's current valuation remains elevated relative to its growth profile. The company trades at 95.7 times earnings, the highest multiple among its peers. That's a steep price compared to a company like Gen Digital, which sells into a related software market and trades at just 17.3 times earnings.

The premium is even sharper when you look at operations. BlackBerry's revenue grew just 2.7% over the last twelve months, while Gen Digital grew 20%. The story is the same for profitability. Is Adobe Stock’s AI Strategy Worth The Near-Term Risk?

A creative software titan is trading at a steep discount, but a major strategy shift has investors wondering if the price is a bargain or a breakdown.

Adobe (ADBE) is the architecture of the modern creative and business world, the company behind Photoshop, Premiere, and the ubiquitous PDF. Yet the market has put a surprisingly low price on this franchise. After a significant markdown, the stock trades at a price-to-earnings multiple of 16.1, a steep discount to the S&P 500 median of 23.3. That kind of gap on a household name forces a question every bargain hunter must answer: is this discount a buying opportunity, or does it reflect market skepticism over slowing growth?

How can a business this profitable be this cheap?

By the numbers, Adobe looks less like a company in trouble and more like a fortress. Its operating margin over the last twelve months was 36%, nearly double the S&P 500 median of 18.5%. This isn't a stagnant business, either; revenue grew 11.5% over the same period, outpacing the broader market.

More importantly, the earnings are backed by cash, and lots of it. The company's operating cash flow margin is a huge 42%, a clear sign of a high-quality, capital-light business model. The fundamentals paint a picture of a dominant enterprise that converts a huge portion of its sales directly into cash. This is the core of the value argument: a highly profitable, growing, cash-generating leader trading well below the market average.

Is a strategic pivot the real reason for the discount?

The value-trap screen found just one flaw: operating margin shrank by a slight 0.3 percentage points over the last year. But the market's real anxiety isn't about that sliver of margin; it's about a deliberate, high-stakes pivot in strategy. Management recently announced a plan to aggressively pursue a "freemium" model for its AI-powered products like Firefly, prioritizing user acquisition over immediate sales. This shift comes at a cost.

Management stated the move "lowers our second half ARR growth expectations from individual subscribers" and involves a decision to "defer previously planned Creative Cloud second half line optimizations." In short, Adobe is trading predictable, high-margin revenue for a long-term bet on converting a large new user base. This strategic gamble is happening during a leadership transition, with an active CEO search underway and an interim CFO in place, adding a layer of execution risk. An investor might wonder what the market's discount is really pricing in, given these moving parts. For those who prefer to invest in the sector as a whole, a broader software ETF like IGV offers an alternative to single-stock risk.

At $314.58, Apple (AAPL) looks set up for roughly 38% of upside over the next three years under a conservative scenario. Not a moonshot, but enough to matter if the math holds. Revenue compounding does all the work, because the scenario holds the multiple flat at today's level rather than assuming any re-rating. Here is the operational reality the math is built on:

The Mac is quietly becoming an enterprise AI workhorse. While the iPhone grabs headlines, the Mac segment is growing an impressive 29% from a year ago. Customers like Disney are now turning to Mac for on-device AI workflows, re-framing the product as far more than a consumer device.

This re-acceleration in a mature product line shows how Apple's massive installed base can ignite new growth cycles. With iPhone revenue up 22% from a year ago, the core hardware business is compounding at a rate that makes top-line growth the primary driver of the stock's potential.

How The Math Gets There

Three projections drive the upside number. Revenue compounds at 12.1% annually over three years, intentionally below today's 14.2% pace, because the recent acceleration is unlikely to extrapolate cleanly over a 3-year horizon. Note this is still above the 6.9% three-year average, so the base case is conservative only relative to the recent spike, not to the multi-year trend. Net margin eases from 28% to 27% as today's LTM reverts partway toward the 3-year average of 26%. The multiple holds near today's 35.8x.

Put those three together and earnings move from $128.9B to roughly $178.1B, a 38% jump. Apply the projected multiple, and the stock lands near $434.54, roughly 38% above today.

Can AAPL Pull That Off?

A new hardware leasing program, Apple Upgrade, could fundamentally alter the upgrade cycle and accelerate revenue. Launched in the U.S. in partnership with Klarna, the program aims to make it easier for customers to get the latest products. Its full impact is not yet reflected in the run-rate.

And what could break it?

The current growth surge faces a significant near-term test from the supply chain. Management warns that the impact from supply constraints is expected to increase significantly in the September quarter. These constraints affect the iPhone, Mac, and iPad, tempering the strong demand picture.

This is a hyper-growth chapter for Palantir Technologies. The company now provides a complete sovereign AI stack, with its AIP platform as the core engine for government and commercial clients.

This explosive U.S. growth is creating immense demand that strains the company's ability to scale. In response, management is now actively searching for technically competent partners to help meet this demand.

That's the story the market is currently paying 147.9x trailing earnings for. Has it taken the multiple too far, or is the growth implied by today's price reasonable? Let's unpack below.

What The Price Is Asking For

To defend PLTR's $446.2B market cap over the next 7 years, three things have to play out. The multiple settles from today's 147.9x toward 28.8x, the multiple a mature, scaled software franchise typically settles into. Margins land near 35%, set near the midpoint of the company's own margin cycle, since its peak clears mature peers but its through-cycle average sits well below that peak. And revenue compounds from $6.2B today to $44.3B at maturity, supporting $15.5B of annual net income. That last line works out to a required revenue CAGR of 33%, below the 79% the business is currently running.

Is This Realistic?

Growth is being driven by accelerating adoption in the U.S. commercial segment. Existing customers are also expanding their use from the Foundry platform to the full Ontology and AI stack. The company is also entering the market for fine-tuning models, expanding its role beyond orchestration.

The company's current growth and margins are at a cyclical peak, far above its historical average. Management has already signaled a significant expense ramp for the coming quarter due to new hiring. This spending, combined with a heavy reliance on the booming U.S. market, creates risk of margin reversion if growth moderates.

Today's price needs less growth than the business is currently delivering. But that current pace is a cyclical peak, not a sustainable rate. In a normal year, the bar is meaningfully higher.

The challenge is finding enough competent partners to scale its U.S. boom before cyclical pressures cause margins to revert.

A one-session jump that its application software peers largely shared says less about Figma than the products it is not yet billing for.

Figma (FIG) stock rose 13.3% on Thursday, from $27.03 to $30.62. That is a move large enough to imply news, but Figma's own announcement the day before was only a notice that its chief executive will speak at an investor conference in September. The direction came from the cohort the stock trades in. What the move did not change is what its guidance has been built to leave out.

Image by StockSnap from Pixabay

A Cohort Bid Explains The Direction, Not The Size

Adobe (ADBE) rose 5.7% over the same session, and Atlassian (TEAM) rose 10.2%, though Microsoft (MSFT) added just 1.8%, against 0.7% for the S&P 500. Application software names do not rise alongside one company on that company's conference notice. What set Figma apart was amplitude, not direction. At $30.62, the stock sits about 57% below its 52-week high of $71.26 and well above the $16.84 low of that span.

The Guide Leaves Out Products The Company Is Already Paying For

The worry is deceleration. Figma's Q3 2026 revenue guidance, given with its August 5 second-quarter results, is $373 million to $375 million, 36% growth at the midpoint, after 48% year-over-year growth in Q2 2026. Some of that step down is a tougher comparison, as the pricing and packaging changes made in March 2025 begin to anniversary. But the guide also excludes Figma agent, Code Layers, and Figma Make on local code, which sit in beta and draw no paid credits. Management is explicit that it is not counting them in the full-year outlook, though the company already bears their inference cost without offsetting consumption revenue. So the guided slowdown carries the cost of the newest products and none of their revenue.

Weekly Agent Use Is Running Ahead Of The Billing

Management says that at the end of July, over 50% of paid customers with more than $10,000 in ARR were using the Figma agent weekly. One of the world's largest technology companies bought an AI credit add-on covering more than 25,000 total paid seats, and now holds more paid seats for engineers than designers. That is the shift the strategy rests on: the buyer moving from the design team to the engineering org. Figma ended Q2 2026 with $1.7 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities, more than its $1.28 billion of trailing-twelve-month revenue. Balance-sheet strength of that kind is what the Trefis High Quality Portfolio looks for in its holdings.

A single-session gain that looks like a verdict on the company's acquisitions arrived with its rivals repricing alongside it, which leaves the company's own test still ahead.

Palo Alto Networks (PANW) stock gained 12.8% on Thursday, closing at $382.85 after falling in six of the seven sessions before it. The easy read is that the market rewarded a shopping spree that has already absorbed CyberArk and Chronosphere. The tape argues otherwise, and the difference decides whether Thursday's move belongs to the company or to the theme.

CrowdStrike Rose Even Harder On The Same Day

A 12.8% session against 0.7% for the S&P 500 looks like company news. Fortinet (FTNT) returned 9.7% in the same session, Zscaler (ZS) 10.0% and CrowdStrike (CRWD) 20.5%, so the largest gainer of the four was a competitor, not the acquirer. What repriced on Thursday was the category, for reasons that reach past any one vendor, and Palo Alto's gain was not even the largest in it. Owning a session like that is owning the security theme rather than the company, a different proposition from the Trefis High Quality Portfolio, which does not depend on the handful of largest technology names to produce its returns.

Inspecting AI Traffic Is Still A Firewall Business

The wager underneath the whole group is that inspecting AI traffic becomes mandatory spending, and on Palo Alto's fiscal Q3 2026 numbers its claim on that is unusually physical. Its largest business is network security, at roughly 70% of revenue, and its sensors sit in line with live traffic, a company-wide footprint of more than 125 million sensors across network, endpoint and cloud taking in over 17 petabytes of telemetry a day. Hardware had its best quarter in a decade, with next-generation firewall bookings up nearly 40% year over year and early wins in AI data centers. Prisma AIRS, its AI security platform, tripled its customer count in a single quarter, but the revenue weight still sits in the firewall line.

The Firewall Boom Is Tied To Data Center Construction

The part that just accelerated is also the most cyclical. Hardware is about 10% of revenue, down from 20% in fiscal 2021, and the bookings surge behind it came from AI data center build-outs, while the 10% hardware price increase taken in early April shows up in the fiscal Q4 and fiscal 2026 outlook instead. Management has said that when data center growth starts to taper off or plateau this demand is going to come to roost, while putting that plateau a few quarters to a few years out, and the company is already watching memory and storage component costs climb.

Intuit's growth came from its existing customers paying more, and the new guide is what winning back volume costs.

Intuit (INTU) reported fiscal Q4 2026 results after the close on August 25, cleared the earnings estimate comfortably, and the stock fell the next trading day. The number that did the damage was not the earnings line: the count of paying customers in Intuit's online business is barely growing.

A 10% Beat Undone By A Guide Below Estimates

Non-GAAP earnings landed at $4.03 a share against a $3.65 non-GAAP consensus, roughly 10% clear, on revenue of $4.35 billion that matched the estimate. The CFO also put fiscal Q4 2026 GAAP earnings at $1.34 a share against $1.35 a year earlier, even as GAAP operating income rose to $475 million from $339 million, so it is the year-over-year earnings growth, not the beat, that lives in the adjustments. Shares fell 3.2% on the first trading day after the report while the S&P 500 was flat, Microsoft (MSFT) rose 0.9%, Oracle (ORCL) rose 2.8%, and Automatic Data Processing (ADP) slipped 0.5% over the same span, so the selling was specific to Intuit's outlook.

Fiscal 2026 Grew On Online ARPC, Not On New Customers

Inside the online business, ARPC growth accelerated to 15% for the year while total online paying customers reached 8.9 million, up 3%, about two points slower than the prior year. Mid-market revenue rose 39% in fiscal 2026, but roughly three-quarters of mid-market customer additions came from upgrades or desktop migrations rather than new names, even though new-to-the-franchise mid-market customers grew over 30%. Pricing the existing base worked less well on the consumer side: management said Intuit lost quality DIY customers to lower-cost providers, with price the leading reason customers leave TurboTax. Profitability was never the problem, with operating margin running at 27.5% against a three-year average of 24.6%. Margin strength of that kind is characteristic of the businesses in the Trefis High Quality Portfolio.

TurboTax Guided To 2% To 3% Growth Is What The Reset Costs

Management guided fiscal 2027 revenue growth to 9% to 10%, against 14% in fiscal 2026, and called the deceleration a deliberate choice. TurboTax revenue is guided to grow 2% to 3% because the company is deliberately accepting lower initial DIY tax ARPC to win filers back on price. On the business side, management calls QuickBooks Free a low-friction entry point for businesses earlier in their journey; the product has drawn more than 20,000 customers, some already converted to paid, against an online paying base of 8.9 million. Management also reset its three-year revenue growth target for the Global Business Solutions segment to 10% to 15% a year.
